headline: Scientists Discover Giant Fungus That Survived 65 Million Years
meta_description: A newly discovered fungus in southwest China challenges what we know about how large fungi can grow, dating back to the age of dinosaurs.
summary_short: Deep in Chinese forests, scientists found 'D-rex'—a fungus tower 20 inches tall that belongs to a family that emerged right after the dinosaurs died out.
body:
In the temperate and tropical forests of Yunnan province in southwest China, an international team of scientists has uncovered a fungal giant that rewrites the record books. The newly identified species, Dianjunnus rex—the "King of Dian"—produces vertical fruiting bodies reaching up to 20 inches high and weighing up to 5 pounds, making it by far the largest ascomycete fungus ever documented. What makes the discovery even more extraordinary is that genetic analysis places the entire family Dianjunaceae at approximately 65 million years old, emerging just one million years after the mass extinction that ended the age of dinosaurs. Researchers from China, Thailand, and Mexico suggest that after that cataclysm opened up ecological niches filled with decomposing wood, fungi like D. rex seized the opportunity to evolve in new ways—and apparently, to grow much, much larger.

The team, led by Dr. Indunil C. Senanayake at the Kunming Institute of Botany, found these whitish fruiting bodies growing on the woody roots of Chinese cork oak. By studying the fungus's morphology and sequencing its genome, they confirmed it represented not only a new species but an entirely new family within Ascomycota, the largest group of fungi on Earth with over 64,000 species. These fungi—which include yeasts that make bread and beer, molds that produce penicillin, and fungi that create prized cheeses and truffles—have shaped human civilization. Yet D. rex stands alone as the undisputed monarch.

Why does this fungus tower so tall? Scientists hypothesize that a fruiting body rising above forest debris gains a decisive advantage: better wind dispersal of spores in dense woodlands. The researchers believe far more fungal discoveries await in East Asian forests, where subtropical ecosystems harbor exceptional biodiversity still largely unknown to science.
quick_facts: Found in Yunnan, southwest China, growing on Chinese cork oak roots
Fruiting bodies reach 20 inches tall, weighing up to 5 pounds
Family Dianjunaceae emerged 65 million years ago, just after dinosaurs went extinct
Scientists from China, Thailand, and Mexico identified the discovery
